dedupe_keys.name: southeastern united states hurricane risk and the finances of 1 030 hospitals

description: This case study examines whether hurricane risk is linked to hospital financial performance, measured by the cost-to-charge ratio, across eight southeastern US states. The authors, researchers at East Carolina University, Florida Agricultural and Mechanical University and the University of North Florida, merged 2021 Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) cost report data with the 2023 FEMA National Risk Index for 1,030 hospitals, excluding federal hospitals, and used multivariate regression; the work is published as an open-access journal article. Coverage is regional at hospital level. Licence (read on 2026-09-29): CC-BY-4.0 (journal article page). Caveats: the analysis is cross-sectional for one year, the model explains about a quarter of the variation, and urban or rural status is self-reported. The study found that higher hurricane risk is associated with lower cost-to-charge ratios, that rural hospitals had 26.5 percent lower ratios than urban ones, and that the quick ratio had a curvilinear relationship with the cost-to-charge ratio, suggesting financial adaptation in high-risk areas. Simulation uses: financial exposure inputs for healthcare system resilience and recovery models. Related records: the CMS hospital cost reports (data-cms-hcris-cost-reports) and the FEMA National Risk Index (data-fema-national-risk-index) are the two datasets the study combines.
